beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Tanishaa, and this video is about RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, and when it actually helps. The voice you're hearing is Bella, an AI narrator reading a script I wrote.

props.command: What is RAG, and when should I actually use it?
output: then answers from what it found.

beats.narration_text: RAG lets an AI look things up before it answers. It doesn't make the model any smarter. It hands the model the right pages, so the answer can point back to a source.

props.text:
RAG makes the AI smarter.
It hands the model the right pages.
props.replacementWords: lets the AI look things up before it answers

beats.narration_text: Start with the problem. A language model answers from patterns it absorbed during training. It has never seen your syllabus, your company handbook, or a policy that changed last month. Ask anyway, and it may still answer, fluently and wrong. Fluent isn't the same as correct.

props.question: Can I submit Lab 3 late?
props.leftAnswer: Yes. Late labs are accepted for up to one week with no penalty.
props.footnote: The “from memory” answer is invented on purpose, to show the failure.

beats.narration_text: RAG adds a step before the answer. Retrieve: search your documents for the few passages that best match the question. Augment: paste those passages into the prompt. Generate: the model writes from that text, and it can say where each part came from.

stages.name: Retrieve
stages.detail: search your documents for the best-matching passages

stages.name: Augment
stages.detail: paste those passages into the prompt

stages.name: Generate
stages.detail: answer from that text, with citations

beats.narration_text: How does the search know which passages match? First, the documents are cut into short chunks. Each chunk is turned into a list of numbers, called an embedding, that captures what it means. The question gets one too. Chunks with similar meaning land close together, so a question about late work can find a passage about an extension.

props.spark: Close in meaning, close on the map.
props.footnote: Schematic: dot positions illustrate the idea; they are not computed embeddings.

beats.narration_text: Here it is on that same question. The search pulls three passages from the syllabus. The top one says labs can be submitted up to forty-eight hours late, with a ten percent penalty. Now the answer quotes it and names the section it came from, so you can check it yourself.

props.question: Can I submit Lab 3 late?

results.text: Labs may be submitted up to 48 hours late with a 10 percent penalty. After 48 hours a lab receives no credit.
Attendance is not graded, but labs are introduced in class and are hard to complete if you miss the session.
Labs are worth 40 percent of the grade, the midterm 25 percent and the final project 35 percent.

props.answer: Yes, within 48 hours of the deadline, with a 10 percent penalty. After 48 hours it gets no credit.
props.citation: Source: §3 Late labs of the syllabus
props.footnote: Example syllabus made up for this demo · scores from demo/rag_demo.py

beats.narration_text: So when should you use it? When the answer lives in documents you can point to, like a syllabus, a manual or last week's meeting notes, especially when those facts change. When shouldn't you? If the document is short, just paste it in. If you need reasoning or writing, not lookup, retrieval won't help much. And watch the search: if it grabs the wrong passage, you get a wrong answer that looks sourced.

the task is reasoning or writing

props.warning: Wrong passage → a wrong answer that looks sourced.

beats.narration_text: Three things to keep. RAG looks things up; it doesn't learn. A citation is something to check, not a guarantee. And the answer is only as good as what was retrieved.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste in a document you actually use and try this prompt: Here's a document I use for school or work. Split it into short passages, show me the three you'd retrieve for my question, then answer using only those passages, quote them, and tell me what the document doesn't say. That last part is the real test. A good answer admits what isn't there.
